concept.name: Dependency Injection

relationships.description: Connects Dependency Injection to jvm internals and garbage collection in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Dependency Injection (DI) flips object creation inside out: instead of a class instantiating its own collaborators with `new`, an external assembler or IoC container supplies those dependencies through constructors or parameters.
spark.keyTakeaway: Prefer explicit constructor injection over field/setter injection so required dependencies are immutable, compiler-checked, and trivially mockable in unit tests.

concept.whyItMatters: Tightly coupled services that call `new PostgresClient()` or read global singletons directly cannot be unit-tested without spinning up real databases, and swapping implementations (e.g., Stripe to Adyen, or S3 to MinIO) forces invasive rewrites across business logic.
whenToUse: Business services that depend on I/O boundaries—databases, HTTP clients, message brokers, clocks, or feature-flag stores—that must be swapped for fakes in fast unit tests.
Multi-module Java (Spring Boot, Micronaut, Dagger 2), Go (Wire), or Python (FastAPI `Depends`) applications with distinct environment bindings (dev vs. prod).
Plugin or multi-tenant architectures where different implementations of an interface are selected at startup or per-request.
whenNotToUse: Pure value objects, DTOs, domain entities, or utility functions with zero side effects (e.g., `Money`, `OrderLine`, `StringUtils`).
Tiny CLI scripts or Lambda handlers under ~300 lines where a 3-argument `main()` function wiring dependencies manually is clearer than a reflection-based DI container.
Ultra-low-latency hot paths (e.g., HFT matching engines) where runtime reflection proxies or dynamic AOP interceptors add unacceptable allocation or dispatch overhead.
keyPoints: Inversion of Control (IoC) is the broader principle; Dependency Injection is the specific mechanism of passing collaborators in rather than pulling them from globals.
Constructor injection guarantees a valid, fully initialized object at creation time and supports `final`/`readonly` fields, preventing partial-state bugs.
Compile-time DI frameworks (Dagger 2, Micronaut, Google Wire) generate wiring code during compilation, catching missing bindings before deployment and eliminating reflection startup latency.
Runtime reflection DI containers (Spring `ApplicationContext`, Google Guice) offer rich lifecycle hooks (`@PostConstruct`, AOP proxies) at the cost of slower cold starts and runtime wiring errors.
The Composition Root—typically `main()` or the app bootstrapper—should be the only place that knows about concrete implementations and container configuration.

examples.title: Spring Boot Payment Gateway Swap Without Touching CheckoutService
examples.scenario: An Indian e-commerce platform migrates UPI/card processing from Razorpay to PayU for 20% of traffic while keeping deterministic unit tests.
examples.outcome: `CheckoutService` depends only on a `PaymentGateway` interface via constructor injection. Spring `@Qualifier` and `@ConditionalOnProperty` route traffic cleanly, and JUnit 5 tests run in 40ms using an in-memory `FakePaymentGateway`.

examples.title: FastAPI Request-Scoped DB Sessions via `Depends`
examples.scenario: A Python ML inference API needs an isolated SQLAlchemy async session per HTTP request that commits on success and rolls back on exception.
examples.outcome: Using `session: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db_session)` with a `yield` generator ensures deterministic cleanup per request and lets `pytest` override `app.dependency_overrides[get_db_session]` with an in-memory SQLite fixture.

tradeOffs.pro: Compile-time DI fails the build on missing/circular bindings and starts in <50ms with zero reflection overhead.
tradeOffs.con: Requires code-generation annotation processors and offers less dynamic runtime rebinding or AOP proxy magic.

tradeOffs.factor: Manual Poor-Man's DI vs. IoC Container
tradeOffs.pro: Zero framework lock-in, explicit stack traces, and crystal-clear object graphs in `main()`.
tradeOffs.con: Once an application exceeds ~40–50 wired services, boilerplate factory code and lifecycle management (shutdown hooks, scopes) become tedious.

tradeOffs.pro: Constructor injection enforces immutability, makes hidden dependencies obvious (bloated parameter lists signal SRP violations), and works without a container in tests.
tradeOffs.con: Slightly more verbose in Java without Lombok `@RequiredArgsConstructor` or Java `record`/primary constructors.

failureModes.name: Captive Dependency (Scope Mismatch)
failureModes.description: A singleton bean holds a reference to a request-scoped or prototype bean (e.g., an HTTP auth context), freezing stale user state across all future requests.
failureModes.mitigation: Never inject shorter-lived scopes directly into singletons; inject a `Provider<T>` / `ObjectFactory<T>` or pass request context as a method parameter.

failureModes.name: Circular Dependency Deadlock
failureModes.description: `OrderService` requires `InventoryService` in its constructor while `InventoryService` requires `OrderService`, causing `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup.
failureModes.mitigation: Extract the shared logic into a third service, introduce an async domain event (`OrderPlacedEvent`), or break the cycle by rethinking module boundaries.

failureModes.name: Service Locator Anti-Pattern Disguised as DI
failureModes.description: Injecting `ApplicationContext` or a global `Container.get(Foo.class)` into business classes hides true dependencies and breaks static analysis.
failureModes.mitigation: Ban `ApplicationContext` injection outside the Composition Root; inject only the specific interfaces each class actually calls.

failureModes.name: Constructor Over-Injection (God Class)
failureModes.description: A service accumulates 9–12 constructor parameters because it orchestrates too many unrelated workflows.
failureModes.mitigation: Treat >5 constructor dependencies as a design smell; split the class into focused domain facades or cohesive use-case handlers.

commonMistakes: Using field injection (`@Autowired private Repo repo;`), which prevents `final` fields and forces reflection hacks in unit tests.
Injecting `Clock.systemUTC()` implicitly inside methods (`Instant.now()`) instead of injecting `java.time.Clock`, making time-dependent tests flaky.
Mocking the DI container itself in unit tests instead of instantiating the class directly with `new MyService(fakeRepo)`.
Creating a `FooInterface` for every single class even when only one concrete implementation will ever exist (premature interface proliferation).
Leaking container annotations (`@Component`, `@Inject`) into pure domain models that should remain framework-agnostic.

sections.content:
## The idea

**Dependency Injection (DI)** separates *object graph construction* from *business behavior*. Instead of a component reaching out to construct or look up its own collaborators (`new HttpClient()`, `Config.getInstance()`), an external **Composition Root** instantiates the concrete implementations and passes them in—ideally via constructor parameters typed to interfaces or abstract ports. This simple inversion decouples high-level policy from low-level I/O, makes every dependency explicit in the type signature, and lets tests substitute fast in-memory fakes without bytecode-mocking frameworks.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace an HTTP request in a Spring Boot / Java service using constructor injection:

1. **Startup (Composition Root)**: Spring scans `@Configuration` classes and builds a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of beans. It instantiates `HikariDataSource` -> `JdbcOrderRepository(dataSource)` -> `OrderService(orderRepo, Clock.systemUTC())` -> `OrderController(orderService)`.
2. **Immutability**: `OrderService` stores `private final OrderRepository repo;` and `private final Clock clock;`. Neither can ever be `null` after construction.
3. **Unit Test (No Container)**: A JUnit 5 test runs `var svc = new OrderService(new InMemoryOrderRepo(), Clock.fixed(...))` in <2ms without starting Spring.
4. **Production Swap**: Switching from `JdbcOrderRepository` to `DynamoOrderRepository` requires changing one `@Bean` / `@Profile` binding in the Composition Root—zero lines change in `OrderService`.

sections.content:
## Lifecycle scopes and captive dependencies

DI containers manage object lifetimes via **scopes**:

- **Singleton** (1 instance per container): Thread-safe stateless services, HTTP connection pools, `ObjectMapper`.
- **Request / Scoped** (1 instance per HTTP request or gRPC call): Per-request DB transactions, tenant/auth context.
- **Transient / Prototype** (new instance per injection): Stateful builders or non-thread-safe buffers.

A **captive dependency** occurs whenever a longer-lived scope (Singleton) captures a shorter-lived scope (Request) in its constructor. Because the singleton's constructor runs only once at startup, it holds onto the first request's object forever. Always bridge shorter scopes using a `Provider<T>` / factory or pass request-scoped data as explicit method arguments.

## Injection styles compared

| Style | Immutability | Null-Safety | Container Required in Tests? | Best Practice Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Constructor Injection** | Yes (`final` / `readonly`) | Guaranteed at init | No (`new Service(fake)`) | **Default choice** for all required dependencies |
| **Method / Parameter Injection** | N/A (per-call) | Explicit at call site | No | Ideal for request-scoped context (`FastAPI Depends`, `Context`) |
| **Setter Injection** | No (mutable) | Risk of `NullPointerException` | No | Use only for genuinely optional callbacks/plugins |
| **Field (`@Autowired`) Injection** | No | Hidden until runtime | Yes (or reflection hacks) | **Avoid**; hides coupling and breaks plain instantiation |

## Failure modes

- **Startup Slowdown from Classpath Scanning**: Broad `@ComponentScan` over thousands of classes in Spring Boot can add 3–8 seconds to cold starts (critical in AWS Lambda / Cloud Run). Use explicit `@Import` configurations or compile-time DI (Micronaut/Dagger).
- **Ambiguous Bean Resolution**: Having two implementations of `CacheClient` (`RedisCache`, `CaffeineCache`) without `@Primary` or `@Qualifier` crashes startup with `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`.
- **Hidden Circular Graphs**: Lazy proxies (`@Lazy`) mask circular dependencies at startup only to cause stack overflows or subtle initialization-order bugs under load.
- **Async Context Loss**: Request-scoped `ThreadLocal` DI proxies fail when work is offloaded to an `ExecutorService` or Python `asyncio.create_task` unless context is explicitly propagated.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Compile-time vs. runtime DI in production
sections.content:
## Compile-time vs. runtime DI in production

In JVM microservices, **Spring Boot** (runtime reflection + CGLIB proxies) dominates enterprise backends where rich ecosystem integrations (Spring Security, Actuator, Kafka) outweigh a 2-second startup. For Android apps, serverless functions, or GraalVM native images, **Dagger 2** or **Micronaut** shift dependency resolution to `javac` annotation processing—eliminating reflection, shrinking memory by 30–50%, and turning missing-bean errors into compiler errors. In Go, **Google Wire** generates plain `InitializeApp()` functions at build time, preserving Go's preference for zero runtime magic.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Use constructor injection for 100% of required collaborators; mark fields `final`/`readonly`.
- [ ] Keep the Composition Root (`main`, `@Configuration`, `wire.go`) isolated from domain packages.
- [ ] Inject `Clock`, `Random`/UUID generators, and `Environment` wrappers instead of calling static globals.
- [ ] Audit any class with >5 constructor parameters for Single Responsibility violations.
- [ ] Never inject a `Request`-scoped bean directly into a `Singleton` without a `Provider<T>` or method-parameter boundary.

interviewProblems.title: Dependency Injection
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Dependency Injection. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Dependency Injection (DI) flips object creation inside out: instead of a class instantiating its own collaborators with `new`, an external assembler or IoC container supplies those dependencies through constructors or parameters.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: PostgresOrderRepo applies the primary invariant and coordinates with InMemoryOrderRepo.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, InMemoryOrderRepo experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Never inject shorter-lived scopes directly into singletons; inject a `Provider<T>` / `ObjectFactory<T>` or pass request context as a method parameter.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Prefer explicit constructor injection over field/setter injection so required dependencies are immutable, compiler-checked, and trivially mockable in unit tests.
Avoid trap: Using field injection (`@Autowired private Repo repo;`), which prevents `final` fields and forces reflection hacks in unit tests.
Avoid trap: Injecting `Clock.systemUTC()` implicitly inside methods (`Instant.now()`) instead of injecting `java.time.Clock`, making time-dependent tests flaky.
When to reach for it: Business services that depend on I/O boundaries—databases, HTTP clients, message brokers, clocks, or feature-flag stores—that must be swapped for fakes in fast unit tests.
When to reach for it: Multi-module Java (Spring Boot, Micronaut, Dagger 2), Go (Wire), or Python (FastAPI `Depends`) applications with distinct environment bindings (dev vs. prod).

putItTogether.title: Putting Dependency Injection Together
putItTogether.summary: Prefer explicit constructor injection over field/setter injection so required dependencies are immutable, compiler-checked, and trivially mockable in unit tests.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Dependency Injection before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: `CheckoutService` depends only on a `PaymentGateway` interface via constructor injection. Spring `@Qualifier` and `@ConditionalOnProperty` route traffic cleanly, and JUnit 5 tests run in 40ms using an in-memory `FakePaymentGateway`.
